title: Only three outside tours of Fort Knox's gold vault have ever been reported

cover.alt: The granite-clad United States Bullion Depository at Fort Knox, Kentucky, a squat fortress-like building behind fences and lawns.

body: The **United States Bullion Depository** at Fort Knox, Kentucky, opened in 1936 and holds about 147.3 million troy ounces of gold, roughly 4,580 tonnes, a little over half of all the gold the US government owns. The bullion arrived by rail in 1937 on 39 trains totalling 215 cars, shadowed by decoy trains and armed Army escorts. Behind a door 21 inches (53 cm) thick and weighing 20 tons, set on a 100-hour time lock, the vault has admitted outsiders on only three reported occasions: President Roosevelt in 1943, members of Congress and the press in 1974, invited in to disprove a rumour that the vault was empty, and a group including Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin in 2017. During the Second World War the vault also sheltered the original Declaration of Independence and Constitution, a Gutenberg Bible and a copy of Magna Carta.

slides.alt: Soldiers and workers moving gold from railcars onto trucks beside a train at Fort Knox in 1941.
slides.caption: 1941: bullion being transferred from railcars to trucks at Fort Knox under Army guard, bound for the depository.
slides.credit: US Post Office Department · Public domain

slides.question: Of every 10 ounces of gold the US government holds, how many sit at Fort Knox?
slides.explanation: About 56%, a little over half: 147.3 million troy ounces, or roughly 4,580 tonnes, in standard bars of about 400 troy ounces each.

slides.heading: Not just gold
items: A Gutenberg Bible and a Magna Carta copy
Hungary's Crown of St Stephen, until 1978
An opium and morphine stockpile, from 1955

slides.label: weight of the vault door, 21 inches thick
slides.text: It is set on a 100-hour time lock, and no visitors are allowed inside.

events.text: Congress and the press see the gold

slides.question: Why did the US Mint open the vault to journalists in 1974?
options: To disprove a claim the gold was gone
To count it for a new audit
slides.explanation: A conspiracy theory claimed the vault was empty. Mint Director Mary Brooks led members of Congress and the news media inside on 23 September 1974 to show the gold.
